title: The risk management process, stage by stage
blurb: Explain the purpose and importance of identification, analysis, monitoring, escalation, response and closure, and read a probability-impact grid.
question: A tram depot upgrade depends on a single power feed, and the team fears an outage during commissioning. Walk the risk through the process: what happens at identification, analysis, monitoring, escalation, response and closure, and why does each stage matter?

teach.h: Six stages that turn worry into action
teach.body: A risk management process is a structured way to find, understand and deal with uncertainty that could affect objectives. The PMQ syllabus names its stages as IDENTIFICATION, ANALYSIS, MONITORING, ESCALATION, RESPONSE and CLOSURE. Plain English: spot it, size it, watch it, pass it up if it's too big for you, act on it, and close it off when it's gone. Skip a stage and the chain breaks: risks are found but never prioritised, or responses are agreed but never checked.

steps.label: Identification
steps.sub: Find and describe risks: cause, event, effect

steps.label: Monitoring
steps.sub: Track triggers, status and new risks

steps.label: Escalation
steps.sub: Beyond tolerance: to sponsor or board

steps.label: Response
steps.sub: Plan and implement actions, with owners

steps.label: Closure
steps.sub: Close passed or occurred risks; lessons

teach.caption: The stages overlap in practice: monitoring runs alongside the others, and escalation can happen whenever a risk exceeds tolerance.

teach.h: Identification: you can't manage what you haven't found
teach.body: PURPOSE: find the risks (threats and opportunities) that could affect objectives, and describe them clearly. Techniques include workshops and brainstorming, checklists and prompt lists (e.g. PESTLE), lessons learned from past projects, reviewing assumptions and constraints, and expert interviews. A good description links CAUSE, EVENT and EFFECT: 'Because the depot has one power feed (cause), an outage may occur during commissioning (event), delaying testing by two weeks (effect).' Each risk goes into the risk register.

teach.h: Analysis: size it so you can prioritise
teach.body: PURPOSE: understand each risk well enough to PRIORITISE it. QUALITATIVE analysis scores each risk's probability and impact on simple scales and plots it on a grid. QUANTITATIVE analysis puts numbers on the combined effect of risks on cost or time, for example through simulation, to judge overall exposure and contingency. IMPORTANCE: effort and money are limited, so analysis points them at the risks that matter most. Proximity (how soon a risk could occur) also affects priority.

teach.caption: Rows are probability (top = most likely). Red risks get attention first. Note that a very high impact stays significant even when unlikely.

teach.h: Monitoring and escalation: watch it, and pass it up when needed
teach.body: MONITORING tracks each risk's status, watches TRIGGERS (early warning signs that a risk is becoming more likely), checks that responses are working and picks up new risks, usually at regular risk reviews. Without it the register goes stale. ESCALATION passes a risk to the sponsor or board when it exceeds the PM's tolerance, needs a decision or resources beyond the PM's authority, or affects other projects. Its importance: the right people decide, in time.

teach.h: Response and closure: act, then tidy up
teach.body: RESPONSE: choose and plan actions proportionate to the risk, then implement them. A RISK OWNER is accountable for managing each risk; an ACTION OWNER carries out a specific response. Without this stage, analysis is just a list. CLOSURE: close a risk when it has passed, has been dealt with, or has occurred (it is then managed as an issue). Closure keeps the register focused, releases linked contingency and captures lessons for future projects.

teach.h: Scenario: one risk at the tram depot

items.label: Identified: single power feed may fail during commissioning
Response planned: standby generator on call; owner named
Monitored: trigger is a utility works notice
Trigger seen: on-site hire exceeds PM tolerance, so escalated; sponsor approves

teach.caption: Real risks don't follow the list neatly: monitoring ran for weeks, and escalation came when a decision went beyond the PM's authority.

teach.text: Classic traps. Don't CLOSE a risk just because a response has been AGREED: close it only when it no longer threatens objectives. Don't confuse identification (finding risks) with analysis (assessing probability and impact). And escalation is not 'send every risk to the sponsor': only those beyond the PM's tolerance or authority.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the stage the question asks about and state its PURPOSE in one sentence.
Explain its IMPORTANCE: what goes wrong if it is skipped or done badly.
Give a practical detail: a technique (workshop, P-I grid), a role (risk owner) or a trigger.
Link it to the next stage, e.g. analysis feeds prioritised responses.
Apply it to the scenario's project, using its named risk.
Identification: find and describe risks (cause, event, effect) in the register.
Analysis: qualitative (P-I grid) or quantitative; prioritise where effort goes.
Monitoring: track status, triggers, response effectiveness and new risks.
Escalation: beyond tolerance or authority, to the sponsor or board.
Response: proportionate actions with a risk owner and action owners.
Closure: when passed, resolved or occurred; release contingency; record lessons.

summary: You can now explain the purpose and importance of each risk management stage, from identification to closure, and use a probability-impact grid to prioritise. You can also say what goes wrong when a stage is skipped, which is what written answers reward.

A.q: What is the main purpose of the analysis stage of risk management?
options: To find risks the team has missed
To carry out agreed risk actions
To assess and prioritise the risks
To confirm a risk no longer applies
A.why: Analysis assesses each risk's probability and impact so the team can prioritise where to focus effort.

whyNot.1: Carrying out actions belongs to the response stage.
whyNot.3: Confirming a risk no longer applies is closure.

A.q: A risk to a new warehouse's opening date has grown and now exceeds the project manager's delegated tolerance. Which stage of the risk process is now required?
options: Identification
Closure
Analysis
Escalation
A.why: Risks beyond the PM's tolerance must be escalated to the sponsor or board, who have the authority to decide.

whyNot.0: The risk is already known; it doesn't need identifying again.
whyNot.1: The risk is growing, not passing, so it can't be closed.
whyNot.2: It has already been assessed; the issue is that it now exceeds tolerance.

A.q: Which of these is the best-written risk description?
options: Because the vendor is at capacity, kits may arrive late, delaying launch
The vendor is at capacity and the team has no control over this at all
Kits arrived late last week, so the launch has now slipped by a month
Late kits are a risk and the project manager should check them weekly
A.why: It links a cause (vendor at capacity), an uncertain event (kits may arrive late) and an effect on objectives (launch delayed).

whyNot.1: This states a fact (the cause) but no uncertain event or effect.
whyNot.2: This has already happened, so it is an issue, not a risk.
whyNot.3: This names a topic and an action but no cause or effect.

B.q: Which activity belongs to the monitoring stage of risk management?
options: Running the first risk workshop
Checking triggers and response progress
Scoring a new risk's probability
Recording lessons learned as a risk closes
B.why: Monitoring tracks risk status, watches early warning triggers and checks that responses are working.

whyNot.3: Recording lessons at the end is part of closure.

B.q: Why is it important to prioritise risks during analysis?
options: So low risks can be deleted at once
So the sponsor never has to be involved
So effort goes to the biggest exposures
So every risk gets the same attention
B.why: Time and money are limited; prioritising points them at the risks with the greatest effect on objectives.

whyNot.0: Lower risks stay on the register and are monitored, not deleted.
whyNot.1: High-priority risks may well need the sponsor's involvement.
whyNot.3: Equal attention is exactly what prioritising avoids.

B.q: A risk on a festival project is assessed as LOW probability but VERY HIGH impact. How should the team treat it?
options: Ignore it, as it probably won't ever happen
Close it at once as not credible
Give it attention despite low probability
Log it as an issue for the sponsor
B.why: A very high impact keeps a risk significant even if it is unlikely; it needs a response or at least a fallback and monitoring.

whyNot.0: Ignoring it leaves the project exposed to a severe effect.
whyNot.1: A plausible risk shouldn't be closed just because it's unlikely.
whyNot.3: It hasn't happened, so it isn't an issue.

C.q: A stadium project logged the risk 'frost may delay the concrete pours'. In spring the pours finish without any frost. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Keep it open in case frost returns next year
Close it, release its contingency, note lessons
Convert it into an issue for the final report
Re-analyse it at the next monthly review
C.why: The risk has passed, so it should be formally closed. Linked contingency can be released through governance and lessons recorded.

whyNot.0: The pours are finished; the risk can no longer affect objectives.
whyNot.2: Nothing happened, so there is no issue.
whyNot.3: Re-analysis is pointless for a risk that can no longer occur.

C.q: Which THREE are reasons to close risks formally? 1. Keeps the register focused on live risks. 2. Releases contingency no longer needed. 3. Captures lessons for future projects. 4. Removes the need to monitor other risks.
options: 1, 2 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 3
C.why: Closure keeps the register current (1), frees contingency through governance (2) and records lessons (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 4 is false: other live risks still need monitoring.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 is false, and 1 is a genuine reason.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false, and 2 is a genuine reason.

C.q: A transport sponsor wants to know how likely the whole programme is to finish within budget, taking all its risks together. Which kind of analysis best answers this?
options: Quantitative analysis of combined effect
Qualitative scoring of each risk alone
A fresh risk identification workshop
Escalation to the portfolio board
C.why: Quantitative analysis models the combined effect of risks on cost or time, giving an overall view of the chance of meeting the budget.

whyNot.1: Qualitative scoring ranks risks one at a time; it doesn't give an overall likelihood for the budget.
whyNot.2: Identification finds risks; it doesn't measure their combined effect.
whyNot.3: Escalation passes decisions up; it isn't a form of analysis.

reteach.title: Think of organising a music festival
reteach.question: A team is running a one-day outdoor music festival. How would each stage of the risk process look for them, and what would go wrong if they skipped it?

blocks.h: From 'what if it rains?' to a tidy wrap-up
blocks.body: The crew brainstorm what could go wrong or right (identification). They rate each by likelihood and severity: a headliner cancelling is unlikely but huge (analysis). They watch weather forecasts and ticket sales (monitoring). Anything costing more than the producer can sign off goes to the promoter (escalation). They book a standby act and lay trackway for mud (response). After the gates close, they close the risks and write down what they learned (closure).

blocks.h: What happens if a stage is skipped
head: Stage
Skip it and…
rows: The headliner risk is never spotted
Time is wasted on trivial risks
No one with authority approves the spend
The risk is known but nothing is done
Money stays tied up; lessons are lost

blocks.text: Agreeing to book a standby act doesn't close the headliner risk. It closes when the headliner has performed, or the festival is over.

explain.body: Find threats and opportunities and describe each as cause, event and effect. Use workshops, prompt lists such as PESTLE, lessons learned, assumption reviews and expert interviews. Record each in the risk register.

steps.label: Cause
steps.sub: Because the depot has one power feed

steps.label: Event
steps.sub: an outage may occur in commissioning

test.q: A new project manager wants to use the experience of earlier, similar projects to find likely risks. Which identification technique fits best?
options: Earned value performance analysis
Stakeholder mapping
Resource levelling
Reviewing lessons learned
test.why: Lessons learned from past projects are a rich source of risks that are likely to recur.

whyNot.0: Earned value measures performance against plan; it doesn't identify risks.
whyNot.1: Stakeholder mapping analyses interest and influence, not project risks in general.
whyNot.2: Resource levelling adjusts a schedule to resource limits.

explain.body: Assess probability and impact. Qualitative: score and plot on a grid to rank risks. Quantitative: model the combined numerical effect on cost or time. Then prioritise.

test.q: On a probability-impact grid, which risk would normally be dealt with first?
options: Low probability, low impact
High probability, high impact
Low probability, medium impact
Medium probability, low impact
test.why: High probability and high impact gives the greatest exposure, so it sits in the top-priority zone.

whyNot.0: This is the lowest-priority corner of the grid.
whyNot.2: Unlikely with moderate impact: a lower priority.
whyNot.3: Moderately likely with low impact: a lower priority.

explain.body: Monitor status, triggers (early warning signs), response effectiveness and new risks at regular reviews. Escalate to the sponsor or board when a risk exceeds tolerance, needs authority the PM lacks, or affects other projects.

test.q: During monitoring, what is a risk trigger (early warning indicator) used for?
options: Showing a risk is becoming more likely
Proving that a risk has been closed
Allocating the risk to an action owner
Calculating the project's total budget
test.why: A trigger is a warning sign that a risk is approaching or becoming more likely, prompting action or a fallback.

whyNot.1: Closure is confirmed separately; a trigger signals a live risk.
whyNot.2: Allocating owners happens at the response stage.
whyNot.3: Budgets are built from estimates and contingency, not from triggers.

explain.body: Response: plan and implement proportionate actions, with a risk owner accountable and action owners doing the work. Closure: when a risk has passed, been dealt with or occurred; release contingency and record lessons.

test.q: Why is the response stage important in the risk management process?
options: It records lessons for future projects
It finds risks not yet on the register
It turns analysis into owned actions
It ranks risks by likelihood and impact
test.why: Response converts understanding into action: agreed, owned measures that change the risk or prepare for it.

whyNot.0: Recording lessons is part of closure.
whyNot.1: Finding new risks is identification (and ongoing monitoring).
